case_info.scenario: A previously healthy woman in her 40s presented with 6 months of bilateral leg edema, insomnia, and myalgias. One month after symptom onset, her creatinine level was 0.80 mg/dL (71 μmol/L) (reference, 0.50-1.19 mg/dL [44-105 μmol/L]) and 24-hour urine protein content was 8.7 g (reference <0.15 g). Kidney biopsy revealed thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with electron-dense deposits, consistent with membranous nephropathy, stage 2. She was treated with 3 days of methylprednisolone (500 mg) and cyclophosphamide (400 mg), followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/d) for 8 weeks, subsequently tapered by 10 mg every 4 weeks. Four weeks after initial treatment, proteinuria had decreased to less than 0.5 g/d, but proteinuria increased to 6.72 g/d when the prednisolone dosage was decreased to 20 mg/d. At current presentation, she had normal vital signs, pitting edema of the ankles bilaterally, mild resting tremor in both hands, and lighter pigmentation of her facial skin compared with other areas of her body (Figure). Laboratory testing revealed a serum creatinine level of 0.88 mg/dL (78 μmol/L) (reference, 0.59-1.28 mg/dL [52-113 μmol/L]); 24-hour urine protein content, 6.91 g (reference, <0.15 g); and serum albumin level, 28.4 g/L (reference, 40-55 g/L). She reported difficulty sleeping, myalgias, and paresthesias in her fingertips. She had no dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, arthralgias, or rash. The patient did not smoke cigarettes, use illicit drugs, or take herbal supplements but had used skin-lightening cream on her face daily for the prior 7 months. Findings of brain and spine magnetic resonance imaging scans, electroencephalography, and electromyography were unremarkable.
case_info.caption: Patient’s face at presentation, showing lighter skin pigmentation compared with her hands.
case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 0.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are

[Clinical case]
A previously healthy woman in her 40s presented with 6 months of bilateral leg edema, insomnia, and myalgias. One month after symptom onset, her creatinine level was 0.80 mg/dL (71 μmol/L) (reference, 0.50-1.19 mg/dL [44-105 μmol/L]) and 24-hour urine protein content was 8.7 g (reference <0.15 g). Kidney biopsy revealed thickening of the glomerular basement membrane with electron-dense deposits, consistent with membranous nephropathy, stage 2. She was treated with 3 days of methylprednisolone (500 mg) and cyclophosphamide (400 mg), followed by prednisolone (1 mg/kg/d) for 8 weeks, subsequently tapered by 10 mg every 4 weeks. Four weeks after initial treatment, proteinuria had decreased to less than 0.5 g/d, but proteinuria increased to 6.72 g/d when the prednisolone dosage was decreased to 20 mg/d. At current presentation, she had normal vital signs, pitting edema of the ankles bilaterally, mild resting tremor in both hands, and lighter pigmentation of her facial skin compared with other areas of her body (Figure). Laboratory testing revealed a serum creatinine level of 0.88 mg/dL (78 μmol/L) (reference, 0.59-1.28 mg/dL [52-113 μmol/L]); 24-hour urine protein content, 6.91 g (reference, <0.15 g); and serum albumin level, 28.4 g/L (reference, 40-55 g/L). She reported difficulty sleeping, myalgias, and paresthesias in her fingertips. She had no dyspnea, chest pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, arthralgias, or rash. The patient did not smoke cigarettes, use illicit drugs, or take herbal supplements but had used skin-lightening cream on her face daily for the prior 7 months. Findings of brain and spine magnetic resonance imaging scans, electroencephalography, and electromyography were unremarkable.

case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury.       not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

4. Frustration
   Definition:

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We

   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the

       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   Definition:

       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."

       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

4. Frustration
   Definition:

case_info.explanation: Mercury toxicity associated with skin-lightening cream B. Check blood for heavy metals The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that proteinuria, insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are characteristic of mercury intoxication, which may occur with use of contaminated skin-lightening products. Because this patient did not have muscle weakness, a muscle biopsy (choice A) is not recommended. Serum protein electrophoresis (choice C) is not indicated because insomnia, paresthesias, and myalgias are not typical symptoms of multiple myeloma or amyloidosis. Membranous nephropathy was diagnosed on prior kidney biopsy, so a repeat kidney biopsy (choice D) is unnecessary. Mercury is a heavy metal that is present in the earth’s crust and exists in elemental, organic, and inorganic forms, all of which may be toxic to humans. Although the pathogenesis is not fully understood, conjugation of mercury to sulfhydryl groups of proteins throughout the body may inactivate enzymes and increase oxidative stress, inflammation, cytotoxicity, apoptosis, and autoimmunity.1The toxic manifestations of mercury depend on its form, dose, route (inhalation, ingestion, dermal absorption, or injection), and duration of exposure.2Exposure to inorganic mercury, which includes mercurous and mercuric salts, can occur in certain industries (eg, mining, chemical and metal processing), via ingestion of mercury-containing medications, or with use of skin-lightening products.3-5Mercury compounds are readily absorbed through intact skin and inhibit melanin production, resulting in lighter skin color.4,6Although the World Health Organization recommends that mercury levels in skin products should not exceed 1 ppm,5skin-lightening products containing mercury levels greater than 1000 ppm are available in the US and other areas of the world.3,6 Some individuals with chronic exposure to inorganic mercury salts are asymptomatic despite high blood levels of mercury.5Others develop symptoms primarily due to effects on the kidneys and central nervous system; such symptoms manifest months to years after initial mercury exposure.5Inorganic mercury deposition in the kidneys often causes nephrotic syndrome due to membranous nephropathy2or, less commonly, minimal change disease.6Common neuropsychiatric effects include headache, dizziness, insomnia, vision changes, depression, anxiety, tremors, paresthesias, and ataxia.5,7 The differential diagnosis of mercury poisoning includes systemic lupus erythematosus, nephrotic syndrome, polyneuropathy, pheochromocytoma, depression, and dementia.5The diagnosis of mercury intoxication is often delayed due to the nonspecific and heterogeneous nature of associated symptoms and lack of clinician awareness about the condition.2,5,8,9Inorganic mercury intoxication should be suspected in patients with nephrotic syndrome and neuropsychiatric symptoms who have a history of mercury exposure or use skin-lightening products. The diagnosis is made based on elevated levels of mercury in urine or whole blood.5 First-line treatment of mercury intoxication due to skin-lightening cream is discontinuation of the product.5Chelation therapy with dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) or D-penicillamine is indicated for symptomatic patients with abnormal urine or blood mercury levels.5Dimercapto-1-propanesulfonic acid may be used for patients who have adverse effects from DMSA.5Although symptoms of mercury intoxication often improve or resolve after chelation, the prognosis depends upon the severity of clinical presentation, concentration of mercury in the product, and duration of use.5 A heavy metal test revealed a blood mercury level of 16.7 μg/L (83.3 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). A random urine mercury level was 22.2 μg/L (110.7 nmol/L) (reference, <2.5 μg/L [12.5 nmol/L]). Although mercury was not listed on the product label, the patient’s facial cream was found to contain 36 000 ppm of inorganic mercury. She discontinued this cream and underwent chelation therapy with intramuscular DMSA (250 mg daily) for 3 days. Three additional rounds of chelation with DMSA were administered over 3 days with a 4-day interval between rounds. Her neurologic symptoms of insomnia, myalgias, and paresthesias resolved after the second round of chelation, and after the fourth round, she had minimal proteinuria (0.5 g/d) and a normal blood mercury level (2.4 μg/L [12 nmol/L]). The patient was discharged home after a 31-day hospitalization. Twelve months after initial presentation, she was asymptomatic, and laboratory tests revealed normal creatinine, albumin, and urine protein levels.

- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge

[Cognitive Burden]

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
